title: ALPFA NJIT App
summary: A chapter mobile app for finding events, meeting the E-Board, and sharing photos.
role: E-Board content updates and app support
verifiedContribution: Added two E-Board profiles, updated member information and headshots, and committed loading-screen layout and dependency fixes.
overview: A collaborative mobile app for the ALPFA NJIT chapter, bringing chapter events, E-Board profiles, and photo sharing into one place.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Give chapter members a convenient place to find events, learn about the E-Board, and engage with the chapter.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I added two E-Board profiles, updated member information and headshots, and committed loading-screen layout and dependency fixes. My project partner, AnabhayanA, owns the repository.

links.label: See my loading-screen and dependency fixes

sections.title: What the team built
sections.text: The app code includes chapter calendar events and reminders, an E-Board directory, and a capture flow for selecting or taking photos and sharing them through a backend. The camera flow includes filters and optional location labels.

sections.title: Status & limitations
sections.text: The project documentation says core features are implemented, with final visual polish, cross-device QA, and production builds still ahead. The separately deployed backend is not included in the repository; I did not retest its integrations for this portfolio.

cardContribution: I added E-Board profiles and headshots and committed loading-screen and dependency fixes.

title: ZipHeatMap
summary: I built MATLAB heat maps that made the department’s donor concentration by ZIP code easier to see and present.
verifiedContribution: Built the MATLAB ZIP-code validation, filtering, and heat-map workflow for department presentations.
overview: I developed ZipHeatMap for my University Advancement operations work. It turns donor ZIP-code data into geographic heat maps so staff can see where most donors are concentrated. The maps made the geographic pattern easier to see and present to department leadership.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: The department needed a clear geographic view of donor concentration by ZIP code that could be used to communicate the distribution at a high level.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I developed a MATLAB application that checks ZIP-code data, matches it to reference coordinates, summarizes and filters the results, and generates heat maps.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: The application matches ZIP codes against a reference spreadsheet, flags invalid or unmatched entries, and summarizes results by state. Staff can filter locations, view ZIP-code frequency on a heat map, and export a map image or plotted data for presentations.

sections.title: Checks & limitations
sections.text: The maps made the geographic pattern easier to see and present to department leadership. The packaged Windows app and its application instructions were not available to rerun or verify during this review. I have no measured time-savings figure or documented leadership decision to report.

sections.title: Privacy
sections.text: The portfolio describes the workflow without publishing donor records, input spreadsheets, or maps based on donor data.

cardContribution: I built ZIP-code heat maps that made donor concentration easier to see and present.

title: Tempo
summary: A collaborative planner that turns tasks, available time, and commitments into a reviewable schedule.
role: Database setup, API checks, and rebuild review
scope: Collaborative hackathon origin · Local rebuild ongoing
verifiedContribution: Configured PostgreSQL connectivity, checked FastAPI operations, and reviewed planning work in the rebuild.
overview: Tempo started as a collaborative planning project. Its published Next.js rebuild combines task and calendar planning with an optional Gemini assistant; manual planning works without an AI key.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Help people fit tasks around commitments and deadlines while keeping them in control of the resulting plan.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: For the earlier hackathon version, I configured PostgreSQL connectivity and checked FastAPI operations. I also worked with a coding agent on the newer rebuild, reviewing the planning and calendar work and its documented checks.

sections.title: Design decisions
sections.text: The rebuild uses a deterministic planner that works without an AI key. People review proposed changes before applying them; calendar files and subscribed feeds are snapshots, not instant two-way sync.

sections.title: What was checked
sections.text: The published rebuild branch’s progress record reports 43 unit, 22 embedded-database, and 10 desktop/mobile browser tests. The browser tests use mocked external services; the project record says live Supabase, Gemini, calendar-feed, and hosted-cron integrations remain unverified. For this portfolio, a mocked manual-planning flow was run locally to capture the interface with fictional data.

links.label: Read rebuild verification and open limits

sections.title: Version & limitations
sections.text: The Next.js rebuild is published on the revamp/tempo-next branch, which GitHub showed three commits ahead of its upstream main when reviewed. The project README says it has no production deployment. The repository’s default main branch remains the earlier React/Vite and FastAPI version; the screenshot’s exact commit is not recorded.

cardContribution: I configured database connectivity, checked FastAPI operations, and worked with a coding agent on the rebuild.

title: Echo Mountain
summary: A browser snowboarding game with downhill runs, aerial tricks, and keyboard or touch controls.
verifiedContribution: Public history attributes the prototype, test additions, and game-mode updates to my GitHub account.
overview: Echo Mountain connects an interest in snowboarding with game development through a browser game with multiple riding modes, aerial tricks, and local records.
cardContribution: I added the prototype and iterated on game modes, controls, and tests.

sections.title: The idea & audience
sections.text: Explore the feel of a snowboard run through movement, jumps, and tricks in a browser, using a keyboard or touch controls.

sections.title: Project context
sections.text: The public repository lists my account as its sole contributor. Its history includes the initial prototype and later feature and test commits. The records do not state whether I used development assistance, so I am not making a claim about that.

sections.title: What was built
sections.text: The updated React/Vite entry uses a side settings panel and offers Downhill, Practice, Trick run, and Halfpipe modes. It includes aerial tricks, pause and a riding guide, lighting choices, touch controls, and browser-local records by mode and difficulty.

links.label: See later mode and test work

sections.title: Checks & screenshot evidence
sections.text: The Node test suite was run locally for this portfolio review and 57 tests passed; the result is recorded in the local review log, not a public CI run. The public README documents how to run the suite, and the test files are linked here.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps
sections.text: The game remains a prototype. Automated checks and local screenshots do not establish performance across all devices or a complete manual gameplay review. The repository’s GitHub Pages URL returned 404 during this review, so the portfolio links to source rather than a playable deployment.

title: Rock, Paper, Scissors
summary: A small game with a bigger question: how do you know a result is right?
verifiedContribution: Defined checks, requested history and streak features, and reviewed gameplay and keyboard replay.
overview: A browser-based game for playing a round against the computer, with recent history and session streaks.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Make each round understandable and dependable: show both moves, return the right outcome, and let someone play again.

sections.title: My contribution & process
sections.text: I agreed on the rules and checks, requested the recent-history and streak extensions, and reviewed a round and keyboard replay. A coding agent implemented changes from the provided starter and ran checks; the project record separates that assistance from my own observations.

sections.title: Decisions
sections.text: Rounds stay independent. Recent games and streaks are kept in a temporary browser session rather than a database or account.

sections.title: What was checked
sections.text: The project record reports checks for all nine outcomes, invalid input, request behavior, and browser replay. Its final local run recorded 38 non-browser and 10 Chromium tests passing, alongside formatting and lint checks.

sections.title: Limitation & next step
sections.text: Refreshing a completed submission can replay the last move. A redirect after submission is a documented follow-up. The record distinguishes automated checks from the round I personally reviewed.

cardContribution: I agreed on the rules and checks, requested extensions, and reviewed gameplay with coding-agent assistance.
